Silicon carbide hot surface igniter from Resideo (Honeywell Home), part number Q3200U1004/U, 120 VAC.

A hot surface igniter lights the burner by glowing rather than by sparking. Line voltage is applied to a silicon carbide element, it comes up to temperature in seconds, and the gas valve opens onto a surface hot enough to ignite the mixture. There is no pilot to go out and no electrode gap to drift.

Silicon carbide is brittle. The most common way an igniter dies is not electrical — it is being touched during service, or being cycled against a burner that is not lighting cleanly. Handle it by the ceramic base and never by the element.

Match by part number. Igniters in this family share the element and differ in the mounting bracket and the appliance they were built for. The lead length and the bracket are what decide whether one fits; the number stamped on the igniter you are replacing is the reliable guide.

Intermittent pilot retrofit kit from Resideo (Honeywell Home), rated to 150 kBtuh, part number Y8610U4001/U.

The kit converts a standing pilot appliance to intermittent pilot: the pilot stops burning between calls for heat and is lit and proved electronically when heat is needed. On an appliance that sits idle through the shoulder seasons, the pilot gas saved is the whole point.

Retrofit kits are rated by appliance input. Fitting one below the appliance rating is not a performance compromise — it is outside what the kit was certified for.

The VR8304P4504 is a two-stage gas control valve from Resideo (Honeywell Home) for intermittent pilot appliances, 24 Vac coil.

The gas valve is the component that admits fuel to the burner and shuts it off. It carries the main shutoff, the pressure regulator that holds manifold pressure steady as supply pressure varies, and the safety interlock that keeps gas off until the control system has proved it is safe to light.

Intermittent pilot lights the pilot only when heat is called for, proves it, and then opens the main valve. Nothing burns between cycles, which is the fuel saving over a standing pilot, and the ignition module watches the flame rod the whole time the burner runs.

The valve is slow opening. A slow-opening valve ramps the burner up over a couple of seconds to soften the light-off; a standard-opening valve goes to full rate at once. Match the opening rate of the valve coming out — this is one of the differences that does not show on the outside of the body.

Two-stage firing lets the appliance run at part load for most of the season and only go to full rate when the load demands it. Longer, gentler burns hold temperature more evenly and cut the cycling losses that come with a single-stage burner switching hard on and off.

Ignition cable assembly from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 30 inch, straight boot, part number 394801-30/U.

The ignition cable carries several thousand volts from the module to the electrode. Its insulation is the only thing keeping that voltage on its intended path, and a cable that has been routed against hot sheet metal for a decade will track to ground long before it looks damaged.

An intermittent spark that gets worse when the blower runs is usually the cable, not the module.

Route the replacement the way the original ran, clear of metal edges and away from the flame path, and seat the boot fully on the electrode. A boot pushed on only part way arcs to the nearest ground instead of across the gap, which reads on the meter as a healthy module and behaves in the field as no ignition.

Length matters as much as fit. A cable cut or coiled to take up slack changes how the circuit behaves at several thousand volts, and the assembly is supplied at the length the appliance was designed around.

Pilot burner from Resideo (Honeywell Home), part number Q345A1305/U, front single-tip style.

The pilot burner holds the small standing flame that lights the main burner and keeps the thermocouple hot. It is a part that does not fail so much as it clogs — lint, rust scale and spider webs in the pilot tube are the classic cause of a furnace that will not stay lit.

The front tip orientation aims the flame at the main burner. Tip direction is not cosmetic: a pilot aimed wrong lights late, heats the thermocouple poorly, or fails to carry over to the burner at all.

Pilot assemblies are sized and aimed for the appliance they were built for, and the catalogue is full of parts that look alike across the bench. Bracket geometry, tube length, tip direction and orifice all have to line up, which is why the part number on the old assembly is worth more than a visual match.

When a pilot problem turns out not to be the burner, it is nearly always upstream of it: a blocked or kinked pilot tube, a thermocouple that no longer makes millivolts, or a draft condition pulling the flame off the thermocouple tip. Replace the assembly, but check the tube and the draft while it is apart.

Compression fitting from Resideo (Honeywell Home) for 1/4 in OD pilot tubing, 0.78 in overall, part number 386449-1/U.

Pilot tubing carries gas at a few inches of water column, and the joint at each end is a compression fitting on soft aluminium or copper line. The fitting is cheap, it is the part most often mangled during a pilot replacement, and a weeping one is a gas leak at head height inside the appliance cabinet.

Fittings differ in overall length even at the same tube size, which is why the number matters — the length is what lets the nut reach the thread on a particular valve body.

Tighten these by feel and not by force. The ferrule sets on soft tube in well under a full turn past snug, and a fitting cranked down crushes the tube, restricting the pilot gas rate rather than sealing it.

Never reuse a ferrule that has already been set on another tube. It has taken the shape of that tube and it will not seal on a new one, which is the usual reason a pilot line weeps after a repair.

Flame sensor from Resideo (Honeywell Home), part number Q354A1018/U, 6.37 in rod height.

The flame sensor is the appliance's proof that the burner is actually lit. A flame conducts current in one direction only, and the control measures that rectified microamp signal. No signal, no gas — the valve closes within seconds.

Most "furnace lights then shuts down" calls end here. Oxide builds on the rod over seasons and chokes a signal that is measured in millionths of an amp. Cleaning buys time; a rod that has thinned or warped needs replacing.

Position is as important as condition. The rod has to sit in the flame envelope through the whole firing range, not just at light-off, and a burner that has been re-shaped by years of service can leave a perfectly good sensor sitting in the wrong place.

Rod height is what makes one sensor different from another in this family. Fitting a taller or shorter rod puts the sensing tip outside the flame and produces exactly the fault the part was meant to fix.

The VR8200H1251 is a single-stage gas control valve from Resideo (Honeywell Home) for standing pilot appliances, 24 Vac coil.

The gas valve is the component that admits fuel to the burner and shuts it off. It carries the main shutoff, the pressure regulator that holds manifold pressure steady as supply pressure varies, and the safety interlock that keeps gas off until the control system has proved it is safe to light.

Standing pilot means a small flame burns continuously and lights the main burner on a call for heat. The thermocouple or thermopile in that flame generates the millivolts that hold the pilot valve open — which is why a standing pilot appliance shuts itself off safely if the pilot goes out, with no electronics involved at all.

The valve is slow opening. A slow-opening valve ramps the burner up over a couple of seconds to soften the light-off; a standard-opening valve goes to full rate at once. Match the opening rate of the valve coming out — this is one of the differences that does not show on the outside of the body.

Gas appliance safety. A gas valve must match the appliance it is fitted to — ignition system, capacity, inlet pressure and gas type. Replacement is work for a licensed gas technician, and the appliance manufacturer's parts list is what decides the correct valve, not the physical fit of the threads. If the replacement does not match, the appliance can fail to light, fail to prove flame, or overfire.
